title: I Stopped Covering Shifts After They Billed My Chair

parts.text: I found the invoice because someone named it FINAL_FINAL_chair_really.pdf. Fourteen hundred dollars. A mesh Aeron from our break room, billed as ergonomic replacement for Kyle. I am thirty-three, IT support, admin access, too much restraint. The chair sat in Kyle's cubicle under a baseball bobblehead that never stops nodding. I walked over with the PDF. "Kyle, did you buy the break room chair?" He did not look up from Slack. "Finance said I could expense a chair." I said, "You expensed our chair." He shrugged. "It's the same chair. Relax." The break room now had a folding stool that wobbled when you reached for sugar. Store-brand sugar, glass jar, coffee-stained lid. I had covered three Fridays so Kyle could take his mom to physical therapy, which was a tee time. Lila from accounting pinged me: you seeing this? I typed, seeing it. Pat clapped my shoulder. "Cover phones Saturday. Kyle's out." I said, "Kyle has a fourteen-hundred-dollar chair." Pat laughed. "Don't be petty." I photographed the faded asset sticker under the seat and changed the location in our laptop tool from BREAKROOM to KYLE-CUBICLE. The system auto-emailed Pat. Kyle's status flipped to in a meeting. Pat's door opened. "Jordan. Now." On his screen: the email, my photo, and a calendar invite Kyle had sent the whole team: Saturday coverage, Jordan's got it. I had never accepted. Pat said, "Fix the location before finance sees." I said, "Finance named the file." Behind me the folding stool finally tipped over.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: Pat wants the asset record erased while Kyle's fake Saturday invite is already on everyone's calendar.

social.video_title: He expensed the break room chair — Part 1/2
social.description: A $1,400 invoice, a folding stool, and a Saturday shift I never accepted. The asset tag under the seat was still there. Would you have moved the location in the system?

parts.text: I did not fix the location. I forwarded the auto-email to finance with one line: confirming physical transfer, no purchase. Then I declined Saturday and set an out-of-office: I am not the overflow chair. Kyle rolled the Aeron down the hall into Pat's doorway like a parade. "You're making this weird," he said. I said, "You billed the company for a chair you stole from the company." Lila arrived with a printout and a grape-smelling highlighter. She had highlighted Jordan in the filename and Kyle in the shipping address, his cubicle. Pat tried a joke. Nobody laughed. Finance clawed back the fourteen hundred from Kyle's next report and mailed a company note about transferring assets versus buying them. Kyle rolled the chair back. The stool stayed two weeks because nobody approved a real replacement, which was at least honest. Saturday the phones rang. I did not answer. Pat called at 9:12. I emailed: I cover documented needs. I do not cover tee times. Monday the bobblehead was gone. Kyle said it fell. I found it in the donation box by the elevator, nodding at old keyboards. I lunched in a catalog chair, $289, asset tag applied by me. Kyle asked if we were good. I said, "The stool wobbled. The invoice didn't." I still have FINAL_FINAL_chair_really.pdf. Some evidence should stay ugly.

social.description: I declined the Saturday invite and let the asset email do the talking. The chair rolled back down the hall. Do you cover shifts for people who bill the furniture?
